Ancient Chinese philosopher traditionally credited as author of the [[Tao Te Ching]] and a founder of [[Taoism]]. The name, also romanized Lao Tzu, is an honorific meaning "old teacher" or "venerable master," not a personal name. Traditional accounts give his personal name as Li Er, identify him with Lao Dan, and record his courtesy name as Boyang.

Those accounts place him in the 6th century BC state of Chu during China's [[Spring and Autumn period]] (c. 770–c. 481 BC), describe him as a keeper of archival records at the Zhou court, and remember him as an elder contemporary of [[Confucius]]. Disillusioned with social decay, he is said to have departed westward through the Hao Pass, dictating the *Tao Te Ching* to the gatekeeper Yin Xi before vanishing. [[Sima Qian]] used the name Lao Dan in his *Shiji* (c. 91 BC).

Modern scholars remain divided over his identity and dates. In the 1920s and 1930s many Chinese and Western scholars rejected the traditional dating in favor of the 4th or 3rd century BC. Some regard the traditional figure as largely or wholly legendary, while others consider a historical Lao Dan plausible. The Guodian Chu Slips, buried around 300 BC, contain approximately 2,000 characters corresponding to about forty percent of the received text, though scholars caution that they do not by themselves resolve how it was composed.

Laozi was claimed as an ancestor of the [[Tang dynasty]] (618–907) and honored as a progenitor of the surname Li. In religious Taoism he was increasingly deified and identified with Laojun, a divine manifestation of the Tao.

Device that emits coherent light through optical amplification based on the stimulated emission of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]]. The word began as an acronym for light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation; the earlier microwave device was called a maser, and Gordon Gould first published the acronym "LASER" in 1959.

The first laser was built in 1960 by Theodore Maiman at Hughes Research Laboratories, using a synthetic [[Ruby|ruby]] [[Crystal|crystal]] pumped by a flashlamp. It drew on theoretical work by Charles H. Townes and Arthur Leonard Schawlow and the optical amplifier patented by Gould. The principle of stimulated emission was first theorized by [[Albert Einstein]] in 1917.

In a lightbulb or star, photons are emitted at random from many energy levels. In a laser, the release of a [[Photon|photon]] is triggered by the nearby passage of another photon of similar energy, and the emitted photon is identical to the first. Both can trigger further emission in a chain reaction. This requires an active laser medium, a material with metastable states that stay excited for a relatively long time, plus an energy source that continues to "pump" it.

Lasers differ from other sources in their coherence. Spatial coherence lets a beam be focused to a tight spot or stay narrow over great distances, and high temporal coherence permits a very narrow frequency spectrum or ultrashort pulses lasting attoseconds.

Applications include fiber-optic communication, [[Optical disc|optical disc]] drives, laser printers, barcode scanners, semiconductor manufacturing, [[Laser cutting|cutting]] and welding, [[Lidar]], and laser surgery. The laser is regarded as one of the greatest inventions of the 20th century.

Classical language of the Italic branch of the [[Indo-European languages]], originally spoken in Latium (now [[Lazio]]) around [[Rome]]. Through the expansion of the [[Roman Republic]] it became the dominant language of the Italian Peninsula and then of the Roman Empire. Its grammar is highly fusional, with inflections for case, number, person, gender, tense, mood, voice, and aspect.

Scholars distinguish several phases. Old Latin, spoken until 75 BC, survives in inscriptions and the comedies of Plautus and Terence. Classical Latin, from about 75 BC to AD 200, was a conscious creation of orators, poets, and historians. Vulgar Latin denotes informal registers, which Cicero termed *sermo vulgi* ("the speech of the masses"); regional change in these between the 6th and 9th centuries produced the distinct [[Romance languages]]. Late Latin is the written form from the 3rd century AD onward.

Latin is often called a "dead language," but it did not undergo language death as formally defined. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire it remained the common language of international communication, science, and scholarship in Europe into the early 19th century. Medieval Latin was used across Western and Catholic Europe from the 9th century to the [[Renaissance]], which developed a classicizing form, the basis for Neo-Latin. Latin is now generally studied to be read rather than spoken.

Latin contributed many words to English, particularly after the [[Norman Conquest]], and its roots recur in theology, the sciences, medicine, and law. Ecclesiastical Latin remains the official language of the Holy See and the Roman Rite of the [[Catholic Church]].

System of rules created and enforced by governmental or societal institutions to regulate behavior; its precise definition is a matter of longstanding debate. It has been variously described as a science and as the art of justice, and it shapes politics, economics, history, and society while mediating relations between people. The word comes from Old Norse *lǫg*, attested in Old English as *lagu*.

State-enforced laws can be made by a legislature, resulting in statutes; by the executive through decrees and regulations; or by judges' decisions, which form precedent in [[Common law|common law]] jurisdictions. A constitution, written or tacit, and the rights it encodes may influence their creation. Legal systems differ between jurisdictions, a subject of comparative law. In [[Civil law (legal system)|civil law]] jurisdictions a legislature or other central body codifies and consolidates the law, while in common law systems judges may make binding case law. [[Religious law]], such as Sharia or Halakha, is used in some religious communities and states and has historically influenced secular law. Customary law rests on communal practice.

The scope of law is commonly divided into two domains. Public law concerns government and society, including constitutional, administrative, and [[Criminal law|criminal]] law; private law deals with disputes between parties in areas such as contracts, property, and torts. The distinction is stronger in civil law countries and less pronounced in common law jurisdictions.

The philosophy of law is known as jurisprudence. Normative jurisprudence asks what law should be, analytic jurisprudence what law is. John Austin called law "the command of a sovereign, backed by the threat of a sanction"; H. L. A. Hart described it as a system of primary and secondary rules; Ronald Dworkin, as an "interpretive concept"; and Joseph Raz, as an "authority." On morality, natural law thinkers such as [[Thomas Aquinas]] and Hugo Grotius held that law reflects moral principles, whereas positivists such as Jeremy Bentham and Austin argued that real law is separate from morality. Hans Kelsen, in 1934, held that law is separate from morality yet endowed with "normativity."

Law's history is closely linked to the development of civilization. Ancient Egyptian law, dating as far back as 3000 BC, was based on the concept of Ma'at. By the 22nd century BC the Sumerian ruler Ur-Nammu had formulated the first law code, and around 1760 BC King [[Hammurabi]] codified Babylonian law and inscribed it in stone. Law also raises issues of equality, fairness, and [[Justice|justice]], and its application is debated in terms of legitimacy and the balance between state power and individual liberty.

Process of acquiring new understanding, knowledge, behavior, skills, values, attitudes, and preferences. The ability to learn is possessed by humans, other animals, and some machines, and there is evidence for some kind of learning in certain plants. Some learning is immediate, induced by a single event such as being burned by a hot stove, but much skill and knowledge accumulates from repeated experiences. Its effects often last a lifetime.

Human learning begins at birth, may start before it, and continues until death through interaction with the environment. Habituation has been observed as early as 32 weeks into gestation, indicating that the nervous system is developed enough for learning and [[Memory|memory]] to occur very early. The subject is studied in educational psychology, neuropsychology, cognitive science, and [[Pedagogy|pedagogy]].

Researchers distinguish several kinds. Non-associative learning is a relatively permanent change in the strength of response to a single stimulus due to repeated exposure; it includes habituation, in which an innate response diminishes when a stimulus is repeated, and sensitization, in which a response is progressively amplified. Associative learning includes classical conditioning, studied by [[Ivan Pavlov]], and operant conditioning, which links voluntary behavior to consequences. Behaviorism was pioneered by figures such as [[John B. Watson]] and B. F. Skinner, and observational learning was theorized by Albert Bandura. Learning that an aversive event cannot be avoided may result in learned helplessness.

[[Play (activity)|Play]] has been approached as a form of learning in which children experiment with the world and learn rules; [[Lev Vygotsky]] held it to be the first form of learning language and communication. Evolutionary research suggests that learning is favored over innate behavior in environments that are neither completely stable nor entirely unpredictable.

Transmissive optical device that focuses or disperses a light beam by means of [[Refraction|refraction]]. A simple lens consists of a single piece of transparent material; a compound lens consists of several simple lenses (elements), usually arranged along a common axis. Lenses are made from materials such as glass or plastic and are ground, polished, or molded to shape. Unlike a prism, a lens can focus light to form an image.

Lenses are used in [[Telescope|telescopes]], binoculars, and cameras, and in glasses that correct defects of vision such as myopia. The word comes from Latin *lēns*, the name of the lentil, because a double-convex lens is lentil-shaped.

Scholars disagree on how widely lenses were used in antiquity. The Nimrud lens, a rock crystal artifact dated to the 7th century BCE, may or may not have served as a magnifying or burning glass. The oldest certain reference to a burning glass is in Aristophanes' play *The Clouds* (424 BCE), and [[Pliny the Elder]] confirmed that burning glasses were known in the Roman period. Between the 11th and 13th centuries "reading stones," primitive plano-convex lenses made by cutting a glass sphere in half, were used. Spectacles were invented in northern Italy in the second half of the 13th century.

Spectacle makers' experiments led to the compound optical [[Microscope|microscope]] around 1595 and the refracting telescope in 1608, both in the Netherlands. Because no single-element lens could bring all colors to a focus, the compound achromatic lens was invented by Chester Moore Hall in England in 1733, an invention also claimed by John Dollond in a 1758 patent. Fresnel lenses, which use less material through concentric annular sectioning, were first fully implemented in a lighthouse in 1823.

Russian novelist, moral philosopher, and count. Born to an aristocratic family at Yasnaya Polyana, he achieved acclaim in his twenties with the semi-autobiographical trilogy *Childhood, Boyhood and Youth* (1852–1856) and with *Sevastopol Sketches* (1855), based on his service as an artillery officer in the [[Crimean War]].

His major novels, *[[War and Peace]]* (1869), *[[Anna Karenina]]* (1878), and *Resurrection* (1899), are often cited as pinnacles of realist fiction. He also wrote novellas, including *The Death of Ivan Ilyich* (1886), as well as plays and essays. [[Virginia Woolf]] called him "the greatest of all novelists." He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature every year from 1902 to 1906 and for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1901, 1902, and 1909; his never being awarded a Nobel Prize remains a major controversy.

In the 1870s he experienced a moral crisis followed by what he regarded as a profound spiritual awakening, outlined in *Confession* (1882). His literal reading of the ethical teachings of Jesus, centered on the Sermon on the Mount, made him a Christian [[Anarchism|anarchist]] and pacifist. After witnessing a public execution in Paris in 1857, he wrote that he would "never serve any government anywhere." His ideas on nonviolent resistance, expressed in works such as *The Kingdom of God Is Within You* (1894), influenced [[Mahatma Gandhi]], [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]], and [[Martin Luther King Jr.]]

His rejection of organized religion and state power led the Russian Orthodox Church's Holy Synod to excommunicate him in 1901, a decree he publicly contested. His renunciation of copyrights and his views on property and marriage also produced conflict within his family.

Italian polymath of the High [[Renaissance]], active as a painter, draftsman, engineer, scientist, anatomist, sculptor, and architect. Born out of wedlock to a notary and a peasant woman in or near Vinci in Tuscany, he was educated in [[Florence]] by the painter and sculptor Andrea del Verrocchio. He later spent much time in the service of Ludovico Sforza in [[Milan]], worked again in Florence and Milan and briefly in Rome, and on the invitation of Francis I spent his last three years in France.

His fame initially rested on painting. Despite many lost works and fewer than 25 attributed major works, including numerous unfinished ones, he created some of the most influential paintings in the Western canon. The *[[Mona Lisa]]* is regarded as the world's most famous painting, *[[The Last Supper (Leonardo)|The Last Supper]]* as the most reproduced religious painting of all time, and the drawing *[[Vitruvian Man]]* as a cultural icon. In 2017 *Salvator Mundi*, attributed in whole or part to Leonardo, sold at auction for US$450.3 million, a record for a painting at public auction. His work is rivalled in its effect on European art only by that of his younger contemporary [[Michelangelo]].

His notebooks contain drawings and notes on anatomy, astronomy, botany, cartography, and palaeontology. They show flying machines, an armored fighting vehicle, concentrated solar power, and the double hull. Few designs were built or feasible in his lifetime, though smaller inventions such as an automated bobbin winder and a machine for testing the tensile strength of wire entered manufacturing. He made substantial discoveries in anatomy, civil engineering, hydrodynamics, geology, optics, and tribology, but did not publish them, and they had little direct influence on later science.

Swiss polymath active as a mathematician, physicist, astronomer, logician, geographer, music theorist, and engineer. Born in [[Basel]], he studied there under Johann Bernoulli, and received a Master of Philosophy in 1723. He spent most of his adult life in [[Saint Petersburg]], Russia, and in Berlin, then the capital of Prussia.

Euler founded the studies of [[Graph theory|graph theory]] and topology, the former partly through the [[Seven Bridges of Königsberg]] problem, also considered the first practical application of topology. He made influential discoveries in analytic number theory, complex analysis, and infinitesimal calculus, and solved the famous Basel problem. He found that for a polyhedron with no holes, vertices plus faces minus edges equals 2, now known as the [[Euler characteristic]].

He introduced much of modern mathematical terminology and notation, including the notion of a function. He popularized the Greek letter π for the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, first used the notation f(x), the letter *i* for the imaginary unit, Σ for summation, and Δ for finite differences, and gave the current definition of the constant [[E (mathematical constant)|e]], now known as Euler's number.

In physics he reformulated [[Newton's laws of motion]] in his two-volume *Mechanica* to better explain the motion of rigid bodies, formulated the partial differential equations for the motion of inviscid fluid, and laid the mathematical foundations of potential theory.

His 866 publications and his correspondence were collected in the *Opera Omnia Leonhard Euler*. [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] said, "Read Euler, read Euler, he is the master of us all." Euler is regarded as arguably the most prolific contributor in the history of mathematics and science, and the greatest mathematician of the 18th century.

Simple machine consisting of a beam or rigid rod pivoted at a fixed hinge, or fulcrum. It is one of the six [[Simple machine|simple machines]] identified by Renaissance scientists. A lever amplifies an input force to provide a greater output force, a gain called mechanical advantage, equal to the ratio of output force to input force.

For an ideal lever, with no friction in the hinge or bending in the beam, power into the lever equals power out. The ratio of output to input force then equals the ratio of the distances from the fulcrum to the points where the forces are applied, a relation known as the law of the lever.

Levers are classified by the relative positions of fulcrum, effort, and resistance (load). In a Class I lever the fulcrum lies between effort and resistance, as in a seesaw, crowbar, or claw hammer; its mechanical advantage may be greater than, less than, or equal to 1. In a Class II lever the resistance lies between effort and fulcrum, as in a wheelbarrow or nutcracker; its mechanical advantage is always greater than 1. In a Class III lever the effort lies between resistance and fulcrum, as in a hoe, tweezers, or a fishing rod; its mechanical advantage is always less than 1.

The earliest known evidence of a lever mechanism dates to [[Ancient Egypt]] c. 5000 BC, in a simple balance scale. In Mesopotamia c. 3000 BC the shadouf, a crane-like device, was invented, and Egyptian workmen used levers to move obelisks weighing more than 100 tons. The earliest surviving writings on levers date from the third century BC and are commonly attributed to [[Archimedes]], who is quoted as saying, "Give me a lever (long enough and a fulcrum on which to place it), and I shall move the world."
